1	# Streaming growth — the map drawing itself
2	
3	## Purpose
4	
5	Until now a map arrived finished. You opened the stored example and seven tiles were already
6	there. This chapter is about the other way in: you type a sentence, and the map **builds itself in
7	front of you** — a reserved rectangle first, then a claim, then the arrow that justifies it, then
8	the next one, out to the things you could trade — with every proposal the rules refused visible on
9	the way past, and a receipt at the end saying what it cost.
10	
11	The growing is not a decoration wrapped around a wait. **The growing is the loading state** (UX-8,
12	FR-5). There is no spinner in this product, and there is no moment where a blank screen turns into
13	a finished picture — because that moment is the "spinner then dump" the anti-patterns list vetoes
14	(PRD §10 anti-pattern 9), and because a map that simply appears hides the half of the work worth
15	watching: our own rules turning the model down.
16	
17	Three things a reader can do after this chapter that they could not before. **Type any sentence and
18	watch what it would cause.** **Name a destination and get a graded path to it, or an honest "no path
19	reaches this" naming the nearest claim that was reached** (FR-7, UX-13). And, **with no model key at
20	all, watch a recorded example run** (record 0012) — the same stream, the same canvas, the same
21	refusals, labelled as a replay everywhere a reader looks.
22	
23	This chapter owns the eight stream events as the browser types them, the `growth` reducer that folds
24	them into a world, the skeleton tile, the refusal strip, the receipt strip, the Verify door's two
25	cards, the input bar, the strip at the foot of the map, and the replay badge. It owns no arithmetic:
26	every number on every one of those surfaces is a field on an event.
27	
28	**Two things in this chapter are decided and not yet built** *(2026-09-21, the usual cadence — the
29	record and the chapter first, then the code)*. The strip at the foot of the map that says what the
30	run is doing, with *Run details* moving into the panel, is **B11** and **decision record 0023**;
31	today that sentence exists and is clipped to a one-pixel box. When a tile may move is **B3** and
32	**INV-workbench.64**, rewritten by **decision record 0024**; today a tile's column is frozen the
33	moment it is first drawn. Both records are `proposed`, and nothing is implemented against a proposed
34	record.
35	
36	---
37	
38	## Data model
39	
40	### The transport, in one paragraph
41	
42	The browser sends `POST /api/generate` and **reads the reply as a stream** rather than opening an
43	`EventSource`. Two reasons, both hard. The request carries a body — the sentence, an optional
44	destination, the reader's own likelihood, a seed — and an `EventSource` can only send a GET with no
45	body. And an `EventSource` reconnects by itself, which would silently re-run a generation and spend
46	the money twice. The wire format is still server-sent events — an `event:` line naming the event and
47	a `data:` line carrying one JSON object — so the whole thing stays readable in a terminal with
48	`curl`. The route, the eight events and their order are `spec/generation/streaming.md`'s, written in
49	this stack's server half; this chapter says what the browser does with them.
50	
51	### The eight events, hand-typed
52	
53	```ts
54	// frontend/src/stream/events.ts
55	//
56	// Written by hand, exactly as `WorldView` was, because the server's description of
57	// itself and this canvas are built at the same time. The server's own copy is
58	// `backend/src/katalyst/engine/events.py`. A type-level test,
59	// `frontend/src/stream/__tests__/eventsMatchSchema.test-d.ts`, fails the build when
60	// the two drift. It cannot pin the eight envelopes — server-sent events have no body
61	// OpenAPI can describe — so it pins every piece they are built from, which are
62	// aliased to the generated types below rather than retyped, and the four shapes that
63	// do travel as JSON: the receipt, the request, the drafted insert and the working.
64	
65	import type { components } from "../api/schema";
66	
67	/** An identifier the engine minted for a claim. Nothing in the browser ever makes one. */
68	export type PropositionId = string;
69	
70	type Proposition = components["schemas"]["Proposition"];
71	type Link = components["schemas"]["Link"];
72	type Violation = components["schemas"]["Violation"];
73	type World = components["schemas"]["World"];
74	
75	/** The run has started. The first thing that arrives, and it arrives at once. */
76	export interface GenerationStarted {
77	  readonly event: "generation_started";
78	  /** The engine's name for this run. What the transcript is asked for by. */
79	  readonly generation_id: string;
80	  /**
81	   * The seed every random draw in this run came from — always a number here, even
82	   * when the request left it out. Whoever chose it, this event is where the browser
83	   * reads it: the one the request sent, or the one `engine/ids.py` minted when it
84	   * sent none, or, on a replay, the one in the recording's header, which wins over
85	   * both. The browser prints what this says and never works out which case it was.
86	   *
87	   * **And by the time it is a number here it may already be wrong.** A seed is
88	   * up to nineteen digits and a browser holds a whole number exactly only up to
89	   * sixteen, so `JSON.parse` has rounded it before any of our code sees it.
90	   * Nothing computes with a seed — it is printed under the map so a reader can
91	   * ask for the same one again — and a rounded seed printed there is a number
92	   * on screen that is simply wrong, in the one place that exists so an answer
93	   * can be had twice.
94	   */
95	  readonly seed: number;
96	  /**
97	   * The same seed, exactly as it was written on the wire: its digits, not a
98	   * number.
99	   *
100	   * Read off the raw text of the `data:` line by the reader, because that is
101	   * the last moment the digits exist. Absent only when a caller handed the
102	   * events over by hand, and then the parsed number is the whole of what is
103	   * known.
104	   */
105	  readonly seed_as_written?: string;
106	  /** The sentence the reader typed, in their own words. */
107	  readonly hypothesis: string;
108	  /** The Verify door's destination, in their words. Null when they used the Explore door. */
109	  readonly target: string | null;
110	}
111	
112	/** One proposal the rules accepted. A claim, its incoming arrows, or both. */
113	export interface ProposalAccepted {
114	  readonly event: "proposal_accepted";
115	  /** Where this sits in the transcript, counting from 0. */
116	  readonly at: number;
117	  /** The new claim, with its identifier minted by the engine. Null for an arrows-only proposal. */
118	  readonly proposition: Proposition | null;
119	  /** Its incoming arrows, identifiers minted by the engine. */
120	  readonly links: readonly Link[];
121	  /** The claims still open to expand. What the skeletons are drawn from. */
122	  readonly frontier: readonly PropositionId[];
123	}
124	
125	/** One proposal the rules refused. An event, never an error. */
126	export interface ProposalRejected {
127	  readonly event: "proposal_rejected";
128	  readonly at: number;
129	  /** What the model wrote. Never minted, never drawn as a tile, only ever quoted. */
130	  readonly claim_in_words: string;
131	  /** The validator's own codes and its own sentences. One per rule broken. */
132	  readonly violations: readonly Violation[];
133	  /**
134	   * The claims still open to expand — the same field the accepted event carries, and
135	   * for the same reason. A claim closed by its third refusal in a row leaves the
136	   * frontier on this event, so its rectangle comes down at once instead of standing
137	   * there waiting for something that is not coming.
138	   */
139	  readonly frontier: readonly PropositionId[];
140	}
141	
142	/** Every number, worked through the finished map, once. */
143	export interface BeliefsPropagated {
144	  readonly event: "beliefs_propagated";
145	  readonly world: World;
146	}
147	
148	/** The Verify door's answer. Emitted only when the reader named a destination. */
149	export interface Verdict {
150	  readonly event: "verdict";
151	  readonly kind: "reached" | "no_path";
152	  /** The steps of the path, in order. Empty on `no_path`. */
153	  readonly path: readonly PropositionId[];
154	  /** The multiplied-out likelihood of those steps (INV-8). Null on `no_path`. */
155	  readonly product: number | null;
156	  /** On `no_path`: the closest claim the map did reach. */
157	  readonly nearest: PropositionId | null;
158	  /** One plain sentence, the engine's own. */
159	  readonly why: string;
160	}
161	
162	/** What the run cost (NFR-6). */
163	export interface Receipt {
164	  readonly event: "receipt";
165	  readonly model: string;
166	  readonly calls: number;
167	  readonly input_tokens: number;
168	  readonly output_tokens: number;
169	  readonly cache_read_tokens: number;
170	  /**
171	   * How many web searches this run made. Billed apart from tokens, so `dollars`
172	   * cannot be accounted for without it — which is why it is a field of its own
173	   * rather than something a reader is expected to infer.
174	   */
175	  readonly searches: number;
176	  readonly dollars: number;
177	  readonly seconds: number;
178	  /** Live, or played from a recording. The only place in the stream this is said. */
179	  readonly mode: "live" | "replay";
180	  /**
181	   * How hard the model was asked to try, as a plain word: `default` when
182	   * nothing was asked for and the service's own applied, otherwise `low`,
183	   * `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` or `max`. A recording is made rich and a live run
184	   * is made fast (Kent, G13), so two maps of the same sentence at the same seed
185	   * can differ for a reason that has nothing to do with the sentence.
186	   */
187	  readonly effort: string;
188	  /** The day the recording was made, as the map writes a day: `2026-09-18`. Null when live. */
189	  readonly recording_date: string | null;
190	  /** A hash of the prompt this run was made against. Null never; it is always known. */
191	  readonly prompt_hash: string;
192	}
193	
194	/** Why the generation stopped. Not whether the Verify door found anything — that is `verdict`. */
195	export interface Done {
196	  readonly event: "done";
197	  readonly reason:
198	    | "reached_terminal"
199	    | "depth_cap"
200	    | "width_cap"
201	    | "claim_cap"
202	    | "spend_cap"
203	    | "refusal_cap"
204	    | "no_terminal";
205	  readonly claims: number;
206	  readonly links: number;
207	  readonly rejected: number;
208	}
209	
210	/** The run broke. One plain sentence, never a stack trace. */
211	export interface Failed {
212	  readonly event: "failed";
213	  readonly message: string;
214	}
215	
216	export type StreamEvent =
217	  | GenerationStarted
218	  | ProposalAccepted
219	  | ProposalRejected
220	  | BeliefsPropagated
221	  | Verdict
222	  | Receipt
223	  | Done
224	  | Failed;
225	```
226	
227	**The `event` field is put there by the reader, not by the server.** On the wire the name is the
228	`event:` line and the payload is the `data:` line, so the payload itself carries no name. The reader
229	joins them — `{ event: name, ...JSON.parse(data) }` — which is what makes `StreamEvent` a union a
230	`switch` can walk. It is also the one place a name the browser does not know can be caught; what
231	happens to one is B6.
232	
233	**Field names are the wire's, in full.** `input_tokens`, not `inputTokens`. A second spelling of a
234	field is a second thing that can drift, and these come straight off the stream and are printed
235	straight onto the screen. The browser's own view model, `WorldView`, keeps its own spellings because
236	it is a different thing with a different life
237	([`diff-view.md`](diff-view.md), *One field, two spellings*).
238	
239	**Two fields the shapes sheet deliberately does not have twice.** `no_path` is on `Verdict` and
240	nowhere else — `Done.reason` says why the *generation* stopped and has no `no_path` among its seven.
241	And `mode`, the recording's date and the prompt hash are on `Receipt` and nowhere else —
242	`GenerationStarted` carries none of them. Two derivations of one line eventually disagree, which is
243	the same rule that moved the retraction badge onto the world ([`diff-view.md`](diff-view.md) B6).
244	
245	**One field the shapes sheet deliberately does have twice, and why that is not the same mistake.**
246	`frontier` rides both growth events. It is not one fact derived two ways; it is one fact restated
247	after every change to it, so that whichever event arrives is enough on its own to redraw the set of
248	open claims. That is what lets a claim closed by its third refusal lose its rectangle immediately
249	rather than at the next accepted proposal, which might never come.
250	
251	### What the browser asks for
252	
253	```ts
254	export interface GenerateRequest {
255	  /**
256	   * The sentence the reader typed — and, with no key, the whole of how the server
257	   * knows which recording to play. See below. Required, and never empty.
258	   */
259	  readonly hypothesis: string;
260	  /** The Verify door's destination, in the reader's words. Absent is the Explore door. */
261	  readonly target?: string;
262	  /** The reader's own likelihood on the hypothesis. Absent when they chose "I don't know". */
263	  readonly user_belief?: Ranged;
264	  /** Only when reproducing a run we were given a seed for. See below. */
265	  readonly seed?: number;
266	}
267	
268	// The route takes `versions` and `worlds` too, both upper-bounded on it, and the
269	// browser sends neither: the engine's own are what every map in this product is
270	// worked out with, and a screen that could ask for fewer would be a screen that
271	// could quietly make one answer cheaper and less certain than the one beside it.
272	// If a reason to send them ever appears it will be a control a reader can see,
273	// not a default they cannot.
274	
275	/** One async generator over the stream. No component talks to the network. */
276	export async function* generate(request: GenerateRequest): AsyncGenerator<StreamEvent>;
277	```
278	
279	**The browser does not invent a seed.** `seed` is optional and the browser sends one only when it is
280	reproducing a run it was handed a seed for — a shared address, a re-run from the transcript. With
281	none, `engine/ids.py` mints one and `generation_started` says which, so the run is reproducible from
282	the moment it starts and the number on screen is still the engine's. On a replay neither matters: the
283	recording's header carries the seed the recorded run used, and that one wins. A seed is not a claim
284	about the world, but it is still a number, and the rule that no number on screen was made up by the
285	browser is easier to keep than to keep checking.
286	
287	**There is no field naming which recording to play, and there will not be.** With no key the server
288	matches the request's `hypothesis` against each recording's own `generation_started.hypothesis` —
289	exactly, after trimming surrounding spaces — and plays the one that matches; nothing matches, and it
290	says so in one plain sentence rather than guessing. So a launchpad card does the one thing any other
291	caller does: it sends its sentence. Nothing in the browser holds a table of file names, nothing
292	numbers the cards, and the live path and the replayed path send byte-identical requests — which is
293	what makes the reviewer's replay evidence about the live route rather than about a second one.
294	
295	`Ranged` — a likelihood with its two range ends, at full precision — is
296	`frontend/src/world/types.ts`'s, the same shape a belief chip takes
297	([`tiles-ports-wires.md`](tiles-ports-wires.md)).
298	
299	### The `growth` reducer
300	
301	```ts
302	// frontend/src/stream/growth.ts
303	//
304	// One pure function from (state, event) to state. It draws no pixels, makes no
305	// requests, and does no arithmetic: every number it holds is a field it was
306	// handed.
307	
308	/** One proposal the rules refused, as the strip beside the map lists it. */
309	export interface Refusal {
310	  /** Its place in the transcript, counting from 0. The engine's number. */
311	  readonly at: number;
312	  /** What the model wrote. Quoted, never drawn as a tile, never given an identifier. */
313	  readonly claimInWords: string;
314	  /** The validator's own sentences, one per rule broken, in the order it gave them. */
315	  readonly reasons: readonly string[];
316	}
317	
318	/** One reserved rectangle at the growing edge of the map. Never a claim. */
319	export interface Skeleton {
320	  /** `skeleton:<claim id>`, or `skeleton:hypothesis` for the first one. A box's name. */
321	  readonly id: string;
322	  /** The one line it carries. The reader's own sentence, or the open claim's words. */
323	  readonly words: string;
324	  /** The open claim this one hangs off. Null for the first. */
325	  readonly after: PropositionId | null;
326	}
327	
328	/** Where a generation is. Each is a different thing on screen, and none is a spinner. */
329	export type Phase = "waiting" | "growing" | "settled" | "stopped" | "failed" | "ended_early";
330	
331	export interface Growth {
332	  readonly phase: Phase;
333	  /** The engine's name for this run. Null until `generation_started`. */
334	  readonly generationId: string | null;
335	  /**
336	   * The seed every likelihood in this run was worked out from, as its digits.
337	   * Null until the run has started, and never worked out here.
338	   */
339	  readonly seed: string | null;
340	  /** The sentence the reader typed, as the run's first event repeated it back. */
341	  readonly hypothesis: string;
342	  /** The destination the reader named, or null on the Explore door. */
343	  readonly target: string | null;
344	  /**
345	   * The map as far as it has been built, in the same view model the canvas already
346	   * draws. Every number slot the engine has not spoken about reads its absence, so
347	   * a half-built map is drawn by the components that already exist, unchanged.
348	   */
349	  readonly world: WorldView;
350	  /**
351	   * One per claim still open to expand. Rebuilt from `frontier` on **either** growth
352	   * event — accepted or refused — and emptied on `beliefs_propagated`, where the
353	   * frontier is empty by definition.
354	   */
355	  readonly skeletons: readonly Skeleton[];
356	  /** Every refusal, in the order they happened. Never trimmed, never summarised away. */
357	  readonly refusals: readonly Refusal[];
358	  /** The Verify door's answer, when a destination was named. */
359	  readonly verdict: Verdict | null;
360	  /** What the run cost. Null until the receipt arrives; never estimated meanwhile. */
361	  readonly receipt: Receipt | null;
362	  /** Why the generation stopped. Null until it does. */
363	  readonly done: Done | null;
364	  /** The one sentence a `failed` event left. Null otherwise. */
365	  readonly failure: string | null;
366	  /**
367	   * Arrows whose two ends are not both on the map yet, held rather than drawn.
368	   * Expected to stay empty — the engine sends a claim and its incoming arrows in
369	   * one event — and kept because a wire with one end nowhere is a picture of a
370	   * thing that is not true.
371	   */
372	  readonly waitingWires: readonly Link[];
373	  /** Event names this build does not know, and how many of each arrived. */
374	  readonly unknown: ReadonlyMap<string, number>;
375	}
376	```
377	
378	**`beliefs_propagated` replaces the world wholesale.** Until it arrives, `world` is the browser's
379	drawing of the proposals it has watched go past — the claims, the arrows, and an absence in every
380	number slot. When the engine's own world arrives it *is* the world, and the drawing is thrown away
381	rather than merged into. A browser that kept its own version beside the engine's would be a second
382	source of truth, and two sources of truth disagree; this way there is nothing to disagree about.
383	
384	**Who turns the engine's `World` into a `WorldView`, and why it is not a second anybody.** The event
385	carries the server's `World` — the shape in `frontend/src/api/schema.ts`, with the day-by-day series,
386	the retractions and the `Mapping`s the engine writes. The reducer's state holds a `WorldView`, the
387	browser's own hand-written view model, where every number slot is a `Known<T>` carrying either a
388	reading or the reason there is none. Between them sits **exactly one function, the one
389	`ApiWorldSource` already calls** on the answer from `POST /api/worlds`
390	([`diff-view.md`](diff-view.md), *The seam — `WorldSource`*). The reducer calls that same function on
391	`world` and nothing else: no second reader, no "just for the stream" variant, no partial conversion
392	that fills a few fields and leaves the rest. Two functions turning one shape into another would drift
393	inside a week and then a generated map and a fetched map would disagree about a number neither of
394	them computed — the exact failure the whole seam exists to prevent.
395	
396	**Nothing in this reducer mints an identifier.** A claim's identifier is minted by
397	`backend/src/katalyst/engine/ids.py` and arrives on the event. The one name the browser makes is a
398	skeleton's, it names a rectangle rather than a claim, and it is thrown away the moment that claim
399	stops being open. That is the shape of PRD §10 anti-pattern 1 on this side of the wire: not a check
400	that nothing minted an identifier, but nowhere for one to be minted.
401	
402	### What a generation looks like on screen
403	
404	Nothing new is added to the page. The screen is the one
405	[`layout-and-zoom.md`](layout-and-zoom.md) and [`diff-view.md`](diff-view.md) already describe: the
406	canvas, and the **dock** beside it that holds the branch panel, the delta rail and the Inspector.
407	A generation puts four sections into that same dock, above the Inspector, in this order — three of
408	them until 2026-09-21, when *Run details* became the fourth:
409	
410	| Section | When it is there | What it holds |
411	|---|---|---|
412	| **The verdict card** | Only when the reader used the Verify door | The graded path, or the honest *no path reaches this* (B7) |
413	| **The refusal strip** | From the first refusal, for the rest of the run | One row per refused proposal, in the validator's own words (B5) |
414	| **The receipt strip** | From the `receipt` event onward | What the run cost, and the mode it ran in (B6) |
415	| **Run details** | From `generation_started` onward *(added 2026-09-21, decision record 0023)* | Where every claim on the map came from: the route, the generation's identifier and the seed. It is a section of the panel and **never a dialog**. It used to be a line of prose at the foot of the map, where it asserted arrivals on a map with nothing on it yet (B11) |

442	## Behaviour
443	
444	Worked on the assignment's first example, the same run `spec/generation/proposals.md` works. A
445	reader types, into the Explore door, the sentence as a person actually types it:
446	
447	> *The Strait of Hormuz is going to open next week.*
448	
449	**That sentence is not a claim yet, and the difference matters on this screen.** It says nothing
450	about how anybody would settle it or by when, so nothing can score it (INV-1, the rule that a claim
451	nobody can check is not a claim). The first thing the engine does is turn it into one — *"The Strait
452	of Hormuz is open to unrestricted commercial transit for 14 consecutive days"*, with its criteria,
453	its judge and its date — and **that** is the claim **H** that lands on the map. So two strings are in
454	play from the first second and the chapter keeps them apart: the **typed sentence**, which is what
455	the skeleton carries and what the request sends, and the **claim**, which is what the tile carries
456	once it arrives. A reader watching their own words become a checkable claim is watching the most
457	auditable step in the whole pipeline, and collapsing the two would hide it.
458	
459	The map that grows is the one the rest of this part works on — the cast is in
460	[`README.md`](README.md): **H** the strait open, **C** the war-risk premium falls, **B** Brent
461	settles below $68, **R** OPEC+ announces restraint, **M1** a Polymarket contract, **M2** an
462	energy-fund claim, **N1** talks resume. B7 uses the Verify door instead, with M1 as the destination.
463	
464	**No number in this chapter is a measurement of a generation, and that is on purpose.** Real runs
465	have been made and what they cost is written down, dated, in
466	[`../../docs/measurements.md`](../../docs/measurements.md), which owns those figures. Where a run's
467	own number would go here — a token count, a cost, how long it took, a likelihood — this chapter says
468	which field it comes from and prints nothing, so a chapter about a screen never goes stale because a
469	model got cheaper.
470	
471	### B1 — The first second: a rectangle, never a spinner
472	
473	The reader presses **Build the map**. Three things happen before any model call has returned.
474	
475	1. The request goes. `generate()` posts and starts reading.
476	2. `generation_started` comes back at once — the engine emits it before its first call, so it costs
477	   nothing to wait for — carrying the generation's identifier, the seed, the sentence as typed, and
478	   the destination if there was one.
479	3. **One skeleton tile is drawn**, in the leftmost column, carrying the reader's own sentence.
480	
481	That third step is the first paint, and it is on screen in the time one round trip to our own server
482	takes. It carries no likelihood, because nothing has computed one; it carries the reader's words,
483	because the reader typed them.
484	
485	**What that first rectangle is standing in for.** One call — the one that turns the typed sentence
486	into a checkable claim. It arrives as an ordinary `proposal_accepted` at `at: 0` with an **empty**
487	`links`, because the hypothesis has nothing before it, and the rectangle becomes H's tile. On the
488	Verify door a second such call follows at `at: 1` for the destination, and it too is an ordinary
489	claim with no arrows in. There is no separate event for either, and the browser needs none: from this
490	side both are the same fact the rest of the run keeps repeating — *the map got bigger*.
491	
492	**NFR-7's wording is corrected here.** It reads *"streaming first-paint within 1s of the first
493	token"*, and this pipeline has no first token to be within a second of: the model boundary returns
494	**one whole proposal per call** (record 0006), and one proposal takes seconds to come back. A budget
495	measured from the first token would be a budget nothing could ever miss, because the thing it starts
496	timing from arrives at the same moment as the thing it times. So the budget is measured from the
497	request being accepted, and what has to be on screen within the second is a skeleton at its column —
498	which is the honest reading of what UX-8 promises anyway. **NFR-7 now reads that way**, amended
499	2026-09-20 in `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` itself, so the two no longer disagree.
500	
501	**There is no spinner anywhere in this product** — not here, not on the launchpad, not on the
502	`insert` route, not while a lazily fetched midpoint chip is in flight. Waiting is always shown as the
503	shape of the thing being waited for: a reserved rectangle where a claim will go, an absence with its
504	reason where a number will go. Checklist `VR2` is the standing check and
505	`test_there_is_no_spinner_anywhere` is the automated one.
506	
507	**And the foot of the screen says, in words, what is being waited for** *(added 2026-09-21, decision
508	record 0023)*. A rectangle says *where* the next claim goes; it does not say that anything is
509	happening, and on a live run the first proposal takes about twenty-three seconds to come back and
510	later ones fifty to a hundred and ten seconds apart. So from the press onward one strip at the foot
511	of the map carries the run's own sentence, and beside it the count of seconds since the last event.
512	That strip is **B11**, and it is the whole of what this chapter says about waiting: no spinner, no
513	bar, no estimate, and nothing that moves except a number that changed because time passed.
514	
515	### B2 — What a skeleton is, and what it never becomes
516	
517	A skeleton tile is **a reserved rectangle**. Not a shimmer, not a pulse, not a grey bar sliding
518	across a card.
519	
520	* **Its box is a tile's box.** 280 pixels wide (`TILE_WIDTH`), 152 tall (`TILE_MIN_HEIGHT`, the floor
521	  of the tile's own clamp), on the eight-pixel grid, with one border at `--hairline`. It is drawn on
522	  `--surface`, not on `--surface-raised`, so it reads as a space held open rather than as a card with
523	  nothing in it. **The border is dashed** — a solid hairline is what a claim's tile has, and a box
524	  the same weight as a tile beside a tile reads as a tile whose text has not loaded.
525	* **It carries two things and nothing else** *(amended 2026-09-21: this said "one line", and the code
526	  draws two)*. A mark reading **held open**, in the smallest type this product allows and no smaller,
527	  so that what the box is is readable rather than inferred — a reader meeting an empty dashed box for
528	  the first time has no way to know it is a promise rather than a fault. And one line: the first
529	  rectangle carries the reader's own sentence, every later one carries *one step on from "…"*,
530	  quoting the open claim it hangs off — so the reader can see not just that more is coming but *where
531	  from*. No chips, no dates, no clippings, no kind silhouette, no badge, and no number of any kind.
532	* **Its only movement is opacity, at most `--duration-fast`.** Nothing scales, pulses, sweeps or
533	  loops. An animated placeholder is a tool pretending to be busy; a held rectangle is a tool saying
534	  where the next thing goes.
535	* **It is not draggable**, like every other tile (INV-workbench.28).
536	
537	**Where skeletons come from — three events, and nothing else.**
538	
539	| Event | What it leaves on screen |
540	|---|---|
541	| `generation_started` | Exactly one skeleton, for the hypothesis, carrying the sentence as typed |
542	| `proposal_accepted` | One skeleton per claim named in `frontier`, each hanging off that claim. The set is **rebuilt**, so a claim that has left the frontier loses its rectangle in the same frame |
543	| `proposal_rejected` | The same, from the same field. A claim closed by its third refusal in a row is gone from `frontier` here, so its rectangle comes down on the refusal rather than waiting for an accepted proposal that may never come |
544	| `beliefs_propagated` | **Every skeleton goes.** The frontier is empty by definition once the map is finished, so there is nothing left for one to stand for |
545	| `failed` | **Every skeleton goes** *(added 2026-09-21)*. A rectangle is a promise that a claim is coming, and after a run breaks nothing is. The claims that were still open are in the working either way, so nothing is lost by taking the boxes down; what is lost by leaving them up is a reader waiting for a claim for ever |
546	| *the body ending with no terminator at all* | **Every skeleton goes** *(added 2026-09-21)*. The same rule, for the case that is not an event: see B3's *a stream that simply stops*, below |
547	
548	So the skeletons on screen are the **frontier, drawn** — rebuilt from whichever growth event arrived
549	last, and emptied when the world lands. That is a fact the stream states, never a guess the browser
550	makes, and it is the whole reason both growth events carry `frontier` rather than only the accepted
551	one.
552	
553	**Two things close a claim and neither makes an event of its own**: the model answering *Stop* on
554	that line, and its third refusal in a row. Both are recorded — a *Stop* leaves a transcript line, and
555	every refusal is already a `proposal_rejected` — and the browser is never *told* a claim closed,
556	because it can read it: the next growth event's `frontier` simply no longer names it. **So no
557	rectangle ever stands where nothing is coming**, and no event exists whose only job is to announce
558	that nothing happened.
559	
560	It is worth saying what the browser therefore *cannot* say. The stream has no "a call has gone out"
561	event, so **one skeleton stands for one claim still open, not for one model call in flight.** Three
562	calls may be out against one open claim and there is still one rectangle. If a later stack wants the
563	count of calls on screen, the stream has to say it; the browser must not count for itself. (Open
564	question 1.)
565	
566	**A skeleton is never a claim.** It has no identifier on the map — its name, `skeleton:<claim id>`,
567	names a rectangle. It never enters `WorldView.claims`, never reaches the network, never appears in
568	the outline view, cannot be selected, cannot open the Inspector, and has no belief chip to leave
569	empty. There is no number on it to be a number nobody computed, because there is no number on it at
570	all.
571	
572	**On Hormuz, three rectangles and then two.** Walking the run in B3's table: after step 3 — the
573	proposal that brings **B**, caused by **C**, with the single arrow `C → B` — the frontier names H, C
574	and B, so three rectangles stand at the growing edge, reading *one step on from "The Strait of Hormuz
575	is open to unrestricted commercial transit for 14 consecutive days"*, *…from "Lloyd's war-risk
576	insurance premium for Gulf transits falls below 0.4%"* and *…from "Brent crude settles below $68 for
577	five sessions"*.
578	
579	**Step 4 takes one of them down, and it is an accepted proposal that does it.** That step adds the
580	arrow `H → B` and no claim at all; H now causes three claims, which is its full width, so H closes
581	and step 4's `frontier` names only C and B. H's rectangle goes on that event — not because anything
582	announced it, but because the frontier stopped naming it. **N1 never had one:** it arrived at step 2
583	as a `not_tradeable` ending, and an ending has nothing downstream of it, so it never joined the
584	frontier in the first place. The map is honest that the chain stops there, and it is honest about it
585	by drawing nothing rather than by drawing something that then disappears.
586	
587	### B3 — The whole run, as the canvas sees it
588	
589	The same generation `spec/generation/proposals.md` B4 writes out call by call, read from this side of
590	the wire. `at` is the transcript position; the last column is what stands at the growing edge **after**
591	that event has been folded in.
592	
593	| `at` | Event | What lands on the canvas | Rectangles standing |
594	|---|---|---|---|
595	| 0 | `proposal_accepted` | **H** — *"The Strait of Hormuz is open to unrestricted commercial transit for 14 consecutive days"*. `links` is empty; the first rectangle becomes this tile | H |
596	| 1 | `proposal_accepted` | **C** and the wire `H → C` | H · C |
597	| 2 | `proposal_accepted` | **N1** and the wire `H → N1`. An ending, so it never joins the frontier and never gets a rectangle | H · C |
598	| 3 | `proposal_accepted` | **B** and the wire `C → B` — one claim, one incoming arrow | H · C · B |
599	| 4 | `proposal_accepted` | **No claim at all**: `proposition` is null and `links` holds the one new wire `H → B`. H reaches its full width here and closes | C · B |
600	| 5 | `proposal_accepted` | **M1** and the wire `B → M1`. A tradeable ending | C · B |
601	| 6 | `proposal_rejected` | Nothing on the canvas; one row on the refusal strip (B5). The frontier is unchanged — this is B's first refusal, not its third | C · B |
602	| 7 | `proposal_accepted` | **M2** and the wire `B → M2`. A tradeable ending | C · B |
603	| — | nothing on the wire | C answers *Stop*; a transcript line and no event | B |
604	| — | nothing on the wire | B answers *Stop*; the last open claim closes | — |
605	| — | `beliefs_propagated` | Every chip fills, at once (B4). Every rectangle goes | — |
606	| — | `receipt` · `done` | The receipt strip; the stop reason, `reached_terminal`, because the last open claim answered *Stop* (B7). `claims=6`, `links=6`, `rejected=1` — count them off the rows above | — |
607	
608	Two things worth reading off that table. **The transcript's numbering has gaps** — a client sees 7
609	and then the closing events, and the two missing positions are the two stops, which make no event
610	because nothing about the map changed. And **no event ever says a claim closed**: the rectangle for H
611	comes down at step 4 because step 4's `frontier` stopped naming it, and the last two come down on
612	`beliefs_propagated`, where the frontier is empty by definition.
613	
614	The map that grows is **not the shipped fixture and does not pretend to be**: six claims where the
615	fixture has seven, and no feedback arrow `B → R`, because a proposal has no `reflexive` field and
616	nothing can propose one. Every chapter in this part works the fixture; this one works the run, and
617	the difference is a fact about generation rather than a discrepancy to smooth over.
618	
619	**Where a claim lands is decided by its causes, not by when it arrived.** The layout is the layered
620	one [`layout-and-zoom.md`](layout-and-zoom.md) owns: a claim sits in a column to the right of
621	everything that causes it. N1 arrives third and lands in column 1; B arrives fourth and lands in
622	column 2. The picture reads causality, and arrival order leaves no trace in it.
623	
624	**A tile keeps its row, and only its row** *(rewritten 2026-09-21, decision record 0024; this said
625	"nothing that is already on screen moves")*. A tile's **vertical** place — where it sits, and its
626	order within its column — is pinned from the moment it is first drawn and is never taken from it
627	while the map grows. That is INV-workbench.23, and it is the half of the pin that does the work of
628	keeping the reader's place. A tile's **column** is not pinned: it is re-read from the arrows on every
629	pass, so when a later arrow proves a claim belongs further right, the claim goes there on that
630	arrival rather than staying put and being drawn with an arrow doubling back into it.
631	
632	**Why the column had to be freed, measured.** Until 2026-09-21 the pin held x as well as y —
633	`readPositions` in `frontend/src/graph/elkGraph.ts` says it in its own words, *a tile that had a
634	position keeps that position, to the pixel* — and the pins were never dropped, because they are
635	dropped only when a box changes height and a tile reserves its belief rail from the first frame
636	(`BELIEF_RAIL` in `frontend/src/graph/geometry.ts`), so the likelihoods landing changes no height.
637	Measured on three real streams through the app's own layout code (analyst UB, 2026-09-21,
638	`plans/ux-round/B-layout.md`): **zero pin drops in 25, 14 and 12 layout passes.** On the Explore run
639	this chapter walks, nothing points backwards and the freeze costs nothing. On the **Verify** door it
640	is acute: the destination claim arrives second with no incoming arrows at all, lands in column 0
641	beside the hypothesis, is pinned there, and ends the run in column 3 with four arrows into it — three
642	of nine arrows on one kept live run pointing right to left, two of five on another. The feedback rule
643	is not involved: `reflexive` is false on every arrow in all three, and a proposal has no `reflexive`
644	field to set.
645	
646	**Every claim the engine sends is still strictly downstream of the map so far** — a `ClaimProposal`
647	brings one claim and the one arrow into it, so that arrow's source is always a claim that already
648	exists — which is exactly the precondition INV-workbench.22 names, and INV-workbench.22 is unchanged.
649	What moves a column is not a claim arriving downstream; it is an **arrows-only** proposal, or a
650	destination that spent the early part of the run with nothing pointing at it. A late arrival still
651	finds a gap, and nothing above it or beside it shifts.
652	
653	**And the map settles once, when the run stops** — see the end of this section.
654	
655	**The layout answers later, and a box waits for its place rather than borrowing one** *(added
656	2026-09-21)*. The layout runs on a background thread, so between a claim arriving on the stream and
657	that claim being drawn there is always a gap — a frame on this machine, most of a second on a tired
658	one. What the map does in that gap is the whole of `frontend/src/graph/onTheGlass.ts`, and it is one
659	rule: **a box is drawn where the layout put it, and a reserved rectangle stands until the claim it
660	was holding a place for is drawn.** Not until the event carrying that claim arrived — those are two
661	different moments, and everything between them would otherwise be a map with a claim on its way and
662	no rectangle anywhere, which is a growing map that has stopped saying where it is going. It is not a
663	corner case: a generated map's frontier is usually one claim wide, so it turns over completely every
664	few proposals, and each turnover is one of these moments.
665	
666	The rectangle goes the instant the map is whole again, so this can never become a way of leaving one
667	up: a rectangle whose claim closed with nothing coming after it — a third refusal, a broken run, the
668	likelihoods landing — goes at once, because then nothing on the map is waiting for a place.
669	
670	**The one box the map places itself is a rectangle, and it is the first.** Before the layout has
671	answered even once the origin is nobody's place: there is nothing to be drawn on top of, and a
672	generation's first paint may not be an empty stage (B1). So the map puts the rectangle held open for
673	the reader's own sentence there itself. It was *the first box* rather than *the first rectangle*
674	until 2026-09-21, and on a machine where the first answer lost its race to the first proposal that
675	box was the claim. Two promises broke at once. The growing edge went quiet, which is what continuous
676	integration read. And the claim was drawn at the origin, which is not where the layout puts the first
677	box of a map — the layout leaves a margin of its own around what it lays out, so the tile then moved
678	by that margin, and **a box drawn anywhere but where the layout put it** is the thing this part
679	refuses outright (INV-workbench.79, anti-pattern 12). How far it moved was read off the page by the
680	end-to-end test itself, which is what caught it: it holds the first tile's place and compares it with
681	itself later in the run. **That reading is now taken before the run stops** *(2026-09-21, decision
682	record 0024)*, because the settle moves every tile on purpose and a reading taken after it would fail
683	by design. What the reading proves is unchanged: a box the layout has not placed is never drawn.
684	
685	**A wire draws only after both of its ends exist.** In practice the engine makes this true by
686	construction, twice over: a `ClaimProposal` brings the claim and the arrow into it in one event, and
687	an arrows-only proposal names two claims that are already on the map. The reducer does not rely on
688	either. An arrow whose two ends are not both on the map goes into `waitingWires` and is drawn the
689	moment the second end arrives. The list is expected to stay empty for ever, and the test that proves
690	the rule **builds** a stream that fills it rather than assuming one cannot exist. A wire with one end
691	nowhere is a picture of something that is not true, and half a wire is worse than no wire.
692	
693	**The wave is the one already budgeted.** Each wire arrives with the propagation wave
694	[`color-motion-type.md`](color-motion-type.md) spends: about 200 milliseconds (`--duration-wave`),
695	its column 60 milliseconds (`--duration-stagger`) after the column before. It is already built —
696	`.canvas[data-arriving="yes"]` in `frontend/src/graph/canvas.css`, with a `wave-<n>` class per
697	column. Growth switches it on per arrival instead of once per map, and adds no fourth animation to
698	the budget of three.
699	
700	**The wart this used to have, and the rule that removed it** *(rewritten 2026-09-21, decision record
701	0024)*. An arrows-only proposal — step 4 above — joins two tiles that are already placed. While the
702	pin was absolute the wire was drawn where they sat rather than the map being re-laid out to suit it,
703	so an arrows-only proposal whose source happened to sit *right* of its target was drawn pointing
704	backwards: honest about where the tiles were and misleading about the argument. On this run it costs
705	nothing either way — H is in column 0 and B in column 2, so `H → B` points rightwards like every
706	other wire. On a Verify run it was three arrows in nine. Now the column is re-read on every pass, so
707	the tile moves and the arrow points the way the argument runs. What it costs is stated plainly: on
708	the two live Verify runs measured, **five tile-moves across three arrivals** and **three across
709	two**; on the committed Hormuz recording, an eighteen-claim Explore run and not the six-claim one
710	walked above, forty-four across fourteen. A tile that
711	moves keeps its row, so nothing changes height on the page and the reader's vertical scan survives.
712	
713	**Then the map settles once, at the moment the run stops.** Whatever takes the run past *growing* —
714	the likelihoods landing, a break, a stream that ends early — clears every pin and lays the map out
715	once, whole. It is **the same moment the canvas already re-frames at**, so the settle and the
716	re-frame cannot come apart: every tile takes its new place in the same frame the chips fill, and then
717	nothing moves again. It is a **cut**, not an animation — the opacity change already budgeted and
718	nothing more — so the budget of three is untouched and under reduced motion it is already a hard cut.
719	`setCenter` on the focused tile runs on every layout after the first (INV-workbench.25), which is
720	what makes one moment where every tile moves bearable: the tile the reader is on does not go anywhere
721	on the glass. Measured: at the settle the wire length falls **11 264 → 5 567 px** on the recording,
722	**5 729 → 2 973** and **2 930 → 1 773** on the two live Verify runs, and no arrow points backwards
723	and none returns into its own column. On the recording that one moment moves 18 tiles of 18, the
724	furthest by 1 968 pixels. This was Open question 2, **answered below**.
725	
726	**A stream that simply stops** *(added 2026-09-21)*. Every stream a reader stayed for ends in exactly
727	one `done` or one `failed`. A body that ends with neither is a dropped connection —
728	[`spec/generation/streaming.md`](../generation/streaming.md): *"a dropped stream is a finished
729	generation with no terminator. The browser says the stream ended early and offers to run it again."*
730	A server restarted, a proxy gave up on a connection it thought was idle, a laptop slept during a
731	ten-minute run: none of those is a fault anybody on this side can name, and none is a `failed` event,
732	because none of them is the run saying anything at all.
733	
734	What the browser does is three things and no more. **The rectangles come down**, which is the other
735	half of *no rectangle ever stands where nothing is coming* — after this, nothing is, and a map left
736	growing for ever is the one screen in this product that lies without saying a word: it is drawn
737	exactly as a map about to change and it is never going to change again. **The map is kept**, every
738	claim and arrow that arrived, with nothing invented to fill the gap and nothing greyed. And **one
739	plain sentence**, in the same line under the map that says why any other run ended, with **the offer
740	to run the same sentence again beside it** — an offer that says on its face what pressing it costs:
741	*run it again — this asks the model again, and spends again* on a copy with a key, and *play it again
742	— this plays the recording again, and spends nothing* on one without. A control that quietly spends
743	money the second time it is pressed is the one control in this product that must say so before it is
744	pressed.
745	
746	It is not folded from an event, because there is no event: the reader of the stream is the only thing
747	that can notice a body ending, and it hands the reducer that fact by name (`theStreamEnded`) rather
748	than by inventing a ninth event the server never sent. The working as far as it got is still readable
749	at `GET /api/generate/{generation_id}/transcript`, which is the whole reason this state keeps the map
750	rather than clearing it.
751	
752	### B4 — Chips resolve last, and they resolve once
753	
754	**While the map grows, every model chip reads *no engine yet*.** The claims that arrive carry their
755	stated `prior`, and the tile never draws a prior — a second number beside the model's would be a
756	fourth voice ([`tiles-ports-wires.md`](tiles-ports-wires.md)). So a growing map is the same picture
757	this part already ships: real claims, real arrows, real provenance marks, and an absence with its
758	reason in every likelihood slot.
759	
760	**When `beliefs_propagated` arrives, they all fill at once.** One event, one world, every number.
761	The chip's own sentence switches from the *stated* pair to record 0014's *computed* pair with no
762	change to the component, because `WorldView.versions` arrives on the same world and that is the one
763	field the chip reads to choose (Kent, K3; `tiles-ports-wires.md`, *What the model chip says about its
764	own range*).
765	
766	**Never per tile, and never twice.** A likelihood that changed four times as its causes arrived would
767	be four numbers nobody computed: the first three would each be the answer to a question about a map
768	that no longer exists. There is exactly one propagation per generation and exactly one
769	`beliefs_propagated` event, so a chip goes from its absence to its number once and stays.
770	
771	**The reveal is not the number-roll.** The third budgeted animation rolls a likelihood from an old
772	figure to a new one, and here there is no old figure — there is an absence. So the chips appear with
773	an opacity change at `--duration-fast` and nothing rolls. The number-roll still has nothing to roll
774	until an edit moves a number, which is this stack's second pull request.
775	
776	### B5 — Every refusal is on screen, in the validator's own words
777	
778	**A rejected proposal is an event, not an error.** Nothing is retried quietly out of sight and
779	nothing is swallowed. The engine may try again — up to three fresh proposals for one open claim,
780	none of them told why the last was refused (Kent, G4; record 0003's dated amendment) — and **every
781	one of those attempts that was refused is on screen.**
782	
783	The refusal strip is one row per refusal, in the order they happened, newest last. A row carries the
784	model's own words on its first line, ellipsized at a word boundary, and beneath them the validator's
785	own sentence — **one per rule broken**, because a proposal that broke three rules and shows one is a
786	refusal the reader has half seen. The rows are short and there are few of them; a run with a strip
787	long enough to need trimming has a prompt problem, not a layout problem.
788	
789	Two rules the strip obeys, both inherited rather than invented. **The sentence is the validator's, as
790	it wrote it** — `spec/graph/validity.md` owns that copy, and its rules for it are that a message
791	names the claim by its words, never by its identifier, and says what is missing rather than that
792	something failed. The browser never composes a sentence about a refusal. And **a refused claim is
793	never drawn as a tile and never given an identifier** — `claim_in_words` is quoted and nothing else
794	is done with it, which is the same rule as B2's.
795	
796	**On Hormuz, at step 6.** Every recording must hold at least one refusal (record 0012), and the map's
797	own shape supplies it. Expanding B, the model proposes an arrow rather than a claim — `B → H`,
798	*cheaper crude reduces the incentive to close the strait*. Read on its own it is a reasonable
799	sentence; added to the map it closes `H → B → H`, because step 4 has already drawn `H → B`. The rules
800	refuse it with exactly one violation, and its message is the validator's, word for word:
801	
802	```
803	proposal 6   refused
804	   "cheaper crude reduces the incentive to close the strait"
805	   These claims form a loop with no delay in it: "The Strait of Hormuz is open to
806	   unrestricted commercial transit for 14 consecutive days" → "Brent crude settles
807	   below $68 for five sessions" → "The Strait of Hormuz is open to unrestricted
808	   commercial transit for 14 consecutive days". Mark the arrow where a market feeds
809	   back on the world as reflexive and give it a delay, or remove one arrow.
810	```
811	
812	Nothing moves on the canvas when that row appears. B is on its **first** refusal, not its third, so
813	step 6's `frontier` still names C and B and both rectangles stay exactly where they were. Step 7 is
814	the same call asked again with a byte-identical prompt — the next call is never told what was wrong
815	— and it comes back with M2.
816	
817	That row is half the product. It is the moment a reader can see that our own code, not the model,
818	decides what the map is allowed to contain — and it says the one thing that would have made the
819	arrow legal, which is the difference between a rejection and an insult.
820	
821	`proposal 6` is `at`, the engine's own position in the transcript, printed so the row can be found
822	again in the Inspector. Selecting the row opens the Inspector's **this generation** section at that
823	line.
824	
825	### B6 — The receipt strip, and where a transcript is read
826	
827	**This answers [`inspector.md`](inspector.md) open question 2.**
828	
829	When `receipt` arrives, the strip beneath the refusals fills in. It prints what the engine sent and
830	adds nothing up:
831	
832	```
833	THIS GENERATION
834	  model            <Receipt.model>
835	  calls            <Receipt.calls>
836	  tokens in        <Receipt.input_tokens>
837	  tokens out       <Receipt.output_tokens>
838	  read from cache  <Receipt.cache_read_tokens>
839	  web searches     <Receipt.searches>
840	  cost             <Receipt.dollars>, in the two places money has
841	  took             <Receipt.seconds> — "the replay took", on a replay
842	  how hard the
843	    model tried    <Receipt.effort>
844	  mode             live
845	```
846	
847	**Money has two places** *(coordinator, 2026-09-21)*. It printed up to four — `$0.6132` — which is
848	the same fake precision checklist `VR4` exists to stop, in the place a reader is most likely to
849	compare two runs: the fourth place is a rounding of a price table, and four places read as a
850	measurement. **And a guard word exactly when it is true** (K2): a run that spent nothing prints
851	`$0.00`, which is a computed zero and reads as one, and a run that spent something and less than a
852	cent prints `<$0.01`, because `$0.00` there would say a run was free when it was not. One function,
853	used by the generation's strip and the insert's alike, so the two cannot come to write a cost two
854	ways.
855	
856	**And `took` says whose clock it is.** On a live run it is how long the run took. On a replay it is
857	how long the **replay** took — a few seconds of paced playback beside a map that took eleven minutes
858	to make — so the row reads *the replay took*. A reader comparing the two figures without that word
859	would conclude this product is two hundred times faster than it is. The recorded run's own duration
860	is not on the wire; when it is, this row can carry it and say which is which.
861	
862	**Amended 2026-09-21 — there are ten readings, and the tenth is how hard the model tried.** A plain
863	word: `default` when nothing was asked for and the service's own applied, otherwise `low`, `medium`,
864	`high`, `xhigh` or `max`. One setting with two pinned defaults behind it — **a recording is made rich
865	and a live run is made fast** (Kent, G13) — so two maps of the same sentence at the same seed can
866	differ for a reason that has nothing to do with the sentence, and a reader comparing one with the
867	other is entitled to see which they are looking at. It is the word the service takes rather than a
868	number, because a number would be this browser translating one thing into another and printing the
869	translation.
870	
871	Four things about it.
872	
873	* **Every one of those is a field.** The browser does not add the two token counts together, does not
874	  work out a cost from a token count and a price, and does not time anything itself. A price table
875	  lives in exactly one module on the server (`engine/pricing.py`) with the day it was read beside it,
876	  and the dollars on this strip came from there. **Searches are a row of their own** because they are
877	  billed apart from tokens: without that row, `dollars` is a number a reader could check against the
878	  token counts and find wrong.
879	* **Checklist `VR4` is about likelihoods.** *"No number shows more than two significant figures, and
880	  none is missing its range"* is the rule that stops a fake-precise `.347` reaching the screen
881	  (NFR-1). A token count, a call count, a duration and a dollar figure are counts and measurements:
882	  they are printed whole, in `--font-mono` with fixed-width digits, and they have no range because
883	  nothing sampled them. The same reading already lets a lag chip say *14 days* and a tile be 280
884	  pixels wide.
885	* **In replay the mode reads `replay`**, the recording's date sits beside it, and `cost` reads what
886	  the rebuilt receipt carries, which is zero. That zero is a computed zero — the recording was played,
887	  nothing was called, so nothing was spent — not an empty slot, and it is printed rather than hidden.
888	* **Before the receipt arrives the strip is not there.** No running estimate, no ticking cost, no
889	  progress bar. A cost nobody has totalled is a number nobody computed.
890	
891	**The working lives in the Inspector, and it is the panel's third subject.** Until now the Inspector
892	opened on a claim or an arrow. It now also opens on the generation itself, and that section holds
